questions.q: Why do most ML algorithms require categorical columns to be encoded as numbers before training?
options: Most algorithms' internals (weighted sums, distance calculations) are built on numeric math and can't operate on text labels directly
Only neural networks require numeric input; other models accept text directly
Categorical columns are illegal in CSV files
Encoding is purely a cosmetic formatting step with no functional purpose
questions.explain: Algorithms like linear regression, neural networks, and nearest-neighbor methods all perform numeric operations internally, so a text category must first be converted into numbers they can actually use.

questions.q: What problem does one-hot encoding avoid that a naive numeric encoding (basic=0, standard=1, premium=2) would create?
options: It avoids implying a false numeric order or magnitude relationship between categories that don't actually have one
It avoids using any memory at all
It avoids ever needing more than one column
It avoids the need for a training set
questions.explain: A naive numeric encoding would make a model treat 'premium' as literally three times 'basic', which is a meaningless relationship; one-hot encoding sidesteps this by giving each category its own independent binary column.

questions.q: When is ordinal encoding the appropriate choice?
options: Ordinal encoding should never be used
Whenever a column has more than two categories
Only for columns with thousands of distinct values
When the categories have a genuine, meaningful order, like low/medium/high risk
questions.explain: Ordinal encoding is appropriate specifically when categories have a real underlying order that a single numeric column can meaningfully preserve — using it on unordered categories invents a false relationship.

questions.q: What mistake can occur if a categorical encoder is fit separately on the training set and the test set (or on the full dataset) instead of fit on train and then applied to test?
options: The model will train faster
No real problem occurs either way
You can end up with mismatched columns between train and test, or a category in test the encoder never learned during training
The encoder will automatically fix any missing values
questions.explain: Fitting separately (or on the full dataset) risks inconsistent column sets between train and test, or leaking information from test categories into the encoding — the encoder should be fit on train only and then used to transform test.

questions.q: Why is one-hot encoding a poor fit for a column with thousands of distinct values, like zip code?
options: It would delete the column automatically
It would silently convert the column to an ordinal encoding instead
One-hot encoding cannot technically be applied to such columns at all
It would create thousands of new binary columns, one per distinct value
questions.explain: One-hot encoding creates one column per unique category, so a very high-cardinality column explodes into an unwieldy number of columns — other techniques, like target encoding, are typically used instead for such cases.
